fetched_contents.text: Advanced oxidation processes for water and wastewater treatment – Guidance for systematic future research 1. Introduction Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) are generally defined as processes that use in situ generated highly reactive radicals for the oxidative degradation of contaminants [1]. The major radical formed in most AOPs is the hydroxyl radical (•OH) [2]. Besides the •OH, reactive oxygen species (ROS) including singlet oxygen and superoxide, radicals derived from persulfate, carbonate or nitrate, other dissolved inorganic constituents, and solvated electrons may be involved in AOPs and affect process kinetics, reaction mechanisms, and product formation [3,4]. Sulfate and chlorine radical-induced oxidations are often also referred to as AOP-like processes [5]. AOPs can be applied during drinking water and wastewater treatment, water reuse applications, brine and leachate treatment, and groundwater remediation, mostly to degrade organic contaminants but also for reduction of natural organic matter, disinfection or as pre-treatment to improve performance of downstream treatment processes [2,[6], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14]]. Radicals for AOPs in water, including •OH, can be generated in many ways, while AOPs can be broadly classified into four categories that include ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOPs. The latter encompass a range of different, often high-energy, physical methods for AOP generation. Given the diversity of AOPs and the wide range of possible applications, research activity and interest into AOPs has been considerably increasing. Beyond AOPs established at full scale, various processes have been tested at pilot scale, while other AOPs are being explored and developed at lab scale (see Fig. 1). For instance, research has been conducted on the development of new materials for catalytic and electrolytic oxidation [15,16]. Similarly, new advanced oxidation processes such as vacuum UV, plasma treatment as well as new oxidants and radical promoters have been proposed and investigated [[17], [18], [19], [20]]. Various alternative process combinations, from centralized treatment approaches to point-of-use-scale, but also reactor designs for catalytic or radiation-driven AOPs have been developed [15,21,22]. A large array of water contaminants, including so-called emerging contaminants, has been investigated to a great extent for their degradability by AOPs [2,23]. Despite several recent reviews on AOPs [2,5,[24], [25], [26]], it can be challenging for individual researchers to obtain a comprehensive insight and to keep track with the most recent developments in AOP research, given the large number of studies published. One needs to be critical when it comes to the prospective applicability of newly developed AOPs [27,28]. Despite extensive research and development, only a few established AOP variants have been developed from lab-to pilot- and full-scale implementation. The suitability of many novel AOPs for water treatment is debatable e.g., due to the utilization of materials with concerning toxicity, lack of long-term stability, or high energy demand [[29], [30], [31]]. Besides such obvious limitations, we hypothesize that flaws in experimental design and planning often hinder the assessment of new solutions and thereby the translation to pilot- and full-scale demonstration. AOP studies with new materials or new radical generation mechanisms often lack critical information that would allow a sound evaluation of the efficiency in real water matrices, including chemical and energy demand. One example are time-based reaction rate constants of target contaminants only but without further information on energy input, oxidant dose, or chemical reactivity of the target contaminant. Another issue can be the choice of adequate reference processes and treatment objectives. For instance, ozonation has been used as reference process to compare oxidative mineralization efficiency. However, a typical treatment target for ozonation is partial oxidation of target contaminants, followed by biofiltration, which has a significantly lower ozone dosage and, thus, energy demand [32,33] and mineralization is not required in most applications. Many studies combine the assessment of new materials and processes with the simultaneous investigation of new emerging contaminants, screening for transformation products, and the analysis of possible toxicological effects. While these aspects provide important information for a detailed understanding and assessment of the process itself, they do not enable an initial evaluation on the applicability and efficiency of the investigated process at larger scale. To streamline research efforts, systematic approaches are needed for an objective assessment of new AOPs for oxidation of emerging contaminants. This tutorial review aims to guide researchers in developing innovative solutions and materials for advanced oxidation. Email: shuitsh@utar.edu.my Contribution: Writing - review & editing, Supervision, Conceptualization, Resources, Funding acquisition, Validation, Project administration, Investigation Search for more papers by this author Hui San Thiam, Hui San Thiam * orcid.org/0000-0002-8952-4630 Department of Chemical Engineering, Lee Kong Chian Faculty of Engineering and Science (LKCFES), Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman (UTAR), Kajang, Malaysia Contribution: Formal analysis, Validation, Writing - review & editing Search for more papers by this author Shiau Foon Tee, Shiau Foon Tee * orcid.org/0000-0002-5089-1548 Department of Chemical Engineering, Lee Kong Chian Faculty of Engineering and Science (LKCFES), Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman (UTAR), Kajang, Malaysia Search for more papers by this author Gulnaziya Issabayeva, Gulnaziya Issabayeva * orcid.org/0000-0002-9845-4005 Department of Chemical Engineering, Lee Kong Chian Faculty of Engineering and Science (LKCFES), Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman (UTAR), Kajang, Malaysia Centre for Advanced and Sustainable Materials Research (CASMR), Sungai Long Campus, Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman (UTAR), Kajang, Malaysia Contribution: Validation, Resources, Writing - review & editing Search for more papers by this author First published: 03 February 2026 Abstract The pulp and paper industry generates high-strength wastewater with elevated chemical oxygen demand (COD) and recalcitrant organics that are difficult to be treated by conventional methods. This study evaluated the practicality of the Fenton advanced oxidation process as a treatment technology for raw industrial paper mill wastewater, addressing the gap in previous optimization studies that mainly used synthetic or pre-treated effluents. The effects of H2O2 concentration (50–70 mmol/L), Fe2+ dosage (4–8 mmol/L), pH (2–6), and reaction time (120–240 min) were investigated and optimized using response surface methodology (RSM). An optimum COD removal of 86.10% could be obtained under the following reaction conditions: 60.80 mmol/L H2O2, 6.98 mmol/L Fe2+, pH 3, and 209 min. In addition to COD reduction, the total organic carbon (TOC) decreased from 111.20 mg/L in the raw effluent to 36.40 mg/L after treatment, indicating significant organic matter mineralization rather than simple phase transfer. Post-treatment sludge characterization by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP–MS) and field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE–SEM/EDX) showed an iron-rich matrix containing Zn, Ni, Pb, As, and Sn, indicating the sludge should be managed as scheduled hazardous waste under Malaysian regulations. To enhance resource circularity, the Fenton sludge was chemically reduced with Na2SO3, achieving 76.90% conversion of Fe3+ to Fe2+. The regenerated Fe2+ yielded 60.80% COD removal in a subsequent Fenton cycle under optimized conditions. Overall, the results demonstrated the feasibility of Fenton oxidation as a primary treatment technology for real paper mill effluent while offering a viable route for partial iron recovery. fetched_contents.text: Advanced oxidation processes for water and wastewater treatment – Guidance for systematic future research Abstract Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) are a growing research field with a large variety of different process variants and materials being tested at laboratory scale. However, despite extensive research in recent years and decades, many variants have not been transitioned to pilot- and full-scale operation. One major concern are the inconsistent experimental approaches applied across different studies that impede identification, comparison, and upscaling of the most promising AOPs. The aim of this tutorial review is to streamline future studies on the development of new solutions and materials for advanced oxidation by providing guidance for comparable and scalable oxidation experiments. We discuss recent developments in catalytic, ozone-based, radiation-driven, and other AOPs, and outline future perspectives and research needs. Since standardized experimental procedures are not available for most AOPs, we propose basic rules and key parameters for lab-scale evaluation of new AOPs including selection of suitable probe compounds and scavengers for the measurement of (major) reactive species. A two-phase approach to assess new AOP concepts is proposed, consisting of (i) basic research and proof-of-concept (technology readiness levels (TRL) 1–3), followed by (ii) process development in the intended water matrix including a cost comparison with an established process, applying comparable and scalable parameters such as UV fluence or ozone consumption (TRL 3–5). Subsequent demonstration of the new process (TRL 6–7) is briefly discussed, too. Finally, we highlight important research tools for a thorough mechanistic process evaluation and risk assessment including screening for transformation products that should be based on chemical logic and combined with complementary tools (mass balance, chemical calculations). Keywords: Advanced oxidation processes, Experimental design, Probe compounds, Trace organic chemicals, Water treatment Highlights * • Critical review of status, potential and future research needs for individual AOPs. * • Guidance for selection of suitable probe compounds and scavengers. * • Basic rules and key parameters for lab-scale evaluation of new AOPs. * • Systematic approach for proof of concept and development of a novel AOP. 1. Introduction Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) are generally defined as processes that use in situ generated highly reactive radicals for the oxidative degradation of contaminants [1]. The major radical formed in most AOPs is the hydroxyl radical (•OH) [2]. Besides the •OH, reactive oxygen species (ROS) including singlet oxygen and superoxide, radicals derived from persulfate, carbonate or nitrate, other dissolved inorganic constituents, and solvated electrons may be involved in AOPs and affect process kinetics, reaction mechanisms, and product formation [3,4]. Sulfate and chlorine radical-induced oxidations are often also referred to as AOP-like processes [5]. AOPs can be applied during drinking water and wastewater treatment, water reuse applications, brine and leachate treatment, and groundwater remediation, mostly to degrade organic contaminants but also for reduction of natural organic matter, disinfection or as pre-treatment to improve performance of downstream treatment processes [2,[6], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14]]. Radicals for AOPs in water, including •OH, can be generated in many ways, while AOPs can be broadly classified into four categories that include ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOPs. The latter encompass a range of different, often high-energy, physical methods for AOP generation. Given the diversity of AOPs and the wide range of possible applications, research activity and interest into AOPs has been considerably increasing. Beyond AOPs established at full scale, various processes have been tested at pilot scale, while other AOPs are being explored and developed at lab scale (see Fig. 1). For instance, research has been conducted on the development of new materials for catalytic and electrolytic oxidation [15,16]. Similarly, new advanced oxidation processes such as vacuum UV, plasma treatment as well as new oxidants and radical promoters have been proposed and investigated [[17], [18], [19], [20]]. Various alternative process combinations, from centralized treatment approaches to point-of-use-scale, but also reactor designs for catalytic or radiation-driven AOPs have been developed [15,21,22]. A large array of water contaminants, including so-called emerging contaminants, has been investigated to a great extent for their degradability by AOPs [2,23]. Despite several recent reviews on AOPs [2,5,[24], [25], [26]], it can be challenging for individual researchers to obtain a comprehensive insight and to keep track with the most recent developments in AOP research, given the large number of studies published. One needs to be critical when it comes to the prospective applicability of newly developed AOPs [27,28]. Despite extensive research and development, only a few established AOP variants have been developed from lab-to pilot- and full-scale implementation. The suitability of many novel AOPs for water treatment is debatable e.g., due to the utilization of materials with concerning toxicity, lack of long-term stability, or high energy demand [[29], [30], [31]]. Besides such obvious limitations, we hypothesize that flaws in experimental design and planning often hinder the assessment of new solutions and thereby the translation to pilot- and full-scale demonstration. AOP studies with new materials or new radical generation mechanisms often lack critical information that would allow a sound evaluation of the efficiency in real water matrices, including chemical and energy demand. Branch report on pulp/paper wastewater and why AOPs are needed

Pulp and paper mill effluent contains a complex mixture of organic and inorganic contaminants, with a strong emphasis on refractory organics. The evidence indicates that pulp and paper mills liberate wastewater composed of high cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, and that effluents have elevated biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), chemical oxygen demand (COD), and chlorinated chemicals [N3-R1][N3-R2]. A separate review also describes medium and high molecular weight organic material found in pulp and paper industry wastewaters [N3-R3], while a paper industry wastewater review states that chemical treatments, including advanced oxidation processes (AOPs), have been widely used to deal with refractory organic pollutants [N3-R4]. The EPA-related source also highlights AOX (adsorbable organic halides), a bulk parameter measuring total chlorinated organic matter in wastewater [N3-R5]. Taken together, the main contaminants are lignin-derived organics, cellulose/hemicellulose fragments, high-COD organics, and chlorinated organics, especially chlorinated organic halides [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

Conventional treatment is insufficient because these contaminants are recalcitrant, persistent, and often toxic. The evidence explicitly states that pulp and paper mills produce high-strength wastewater with elevated COD and recalcitrant organics that are difficult to treat by conventional methods [N4-F3]. Another source says that advanced oxidation processes are used to deal with a large number of refractory organics pollutants [N3-R4]. This implies that conventional biological or physical-chemical treatment alone cannot achieve sufficient mineralization or removal of the persistent organic load in paper mill wastewater [N3-R2][N3-R4]. In particular, chlorinated organics and AOX are problematic because they resist biodegradation and can accumulate or persist in treatment systems [N3-R2][N3-R5].

AOPs are needed because they address these specific pollutants through radical-based oxidation. The evidence shows that AOPs are used for oxidative degradation of contaminants, including chlorinated organics [N1-R2][N4-F3]. In the case of pulp and paper wastewater, Fenton-based treatment was reported to substantially reduce organic-matter indicators, indicating that AOPs can break down the refractory organics that conventional treatment cannot [N4-R1]. The real-case study on raw paper mill wastewater also found significant organic matter mineralization rather than simple phase transfer after Fenton oxidation, which is a strong indicator that AOPs are effective against persistent organic pollutants [N4-F3]. For chlorinated organics, AOPs are especially relevant because they generate reactive radicals that can oxidize halogenated compounds, including AOX, which are difficult to remove with conventional methods [N3-R2][N3-R5]. The branch evidence also supports the idea that AOPs are used specifically for refractory organic pollutants in paper mill wastewater [N3-R4].

Overall, pulp/paper wastewater is challenging because it contains high-COD, high-molecular-weight organics and chlorinated organics, and conventional treatment is insufficient to remove them effectively. AOPs are needed because they can mineralize recalcitrant organics and oxidize chlorinated contaminants, making them a practical choice for this type of wastewater [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4][N4-F3].

Branch report on common AOP types and their chemical functions

The most frequently used AOP types in wastewater treatment are ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOP variants, with the evidence explicitly stating that common AOP configurations include Fenton and photo-Fenton systems, in addition to ozone/UV, TiO2/UV photocatalysis, and Electro-Fenton systems [N1-R4]. The general review also lists ozone, UV/H2O2, TiO2-assisted photocatalysis, ozonation, Fenton, photo-Fenton, hydrogen peroxide, and electro-oxidation as AOP examples [N1-R3]. These are therefore the most commonly used categories in wastewater treatment literature [N1-R3][N1-R4].

The chemical functions of these AOPs depend on the reactive species they generate. Most AOPs produce hydroxyl radicals (•OH), which are the major radicals in most AOPs [N1-F1][N5-F4]. The review also notes that reactive oxygen species (ROS), including singlet oxygen, superoxide, and radicals derived from persulfate, carbonate, or nitrate, may be involved [N1-F1][N5-F4]. In addition to •OH, sulfate radicals (SO4•−) are also a major pathway in AOPs, and the evidence explicitly compares hydroxyl-radical-based AOPs (HR-AOP) with sulfate-radical-based AOPs (SR-AOP) [N2-F2]. This means that AOPs are not limited to •OH; sulfate radicals are also important, especially in SR-AOP systems [N2-F2].

Each process oxidizes pollutants through radical attack. The general AOP definition emphasizes that AOPs use in situ generated highly reactive radicals for oxidative degradation of contaminants [N1-F1]. The evidence further explains that radicals can be generated through various means, including ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOPs, and that AOPs can be broadly classified into four categories: ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOPs [N1-F1][N1-R4]. In practice, the most important mechanisms are:

- **Fenton and photo-Fenton**: These generate •OH from H2O2 and Fe²+ [N1-R3][N2-F2]. Fenton oxidation is explicitly mentioned as a primary treatment technology in paper mill wastewater, with evidence showing its ability to reduce COD and organic matter [N4-R1][N4-F3].
- **UV/H2O2 (UV/peroxide)**: This is a classic AOP configuration, and the evidence lists it as a common AOP alongside Fenton and photo-Fenton [N1-R3][N1-R4]. It is also used in paper mill wastewater treatment, including in studies of biorefractory retentate and raw effluent [N4-R3][N4-R5].
- **Ozone-based AOPs**: Ozone is a central AOP oxidant, and the evidence explicitly states that ozone-based processes are among the common AOP categories [N1-F1][N1-R3].
- **Photo-Fenton and electro-Fenton**: These are catalytic AOP variants that use light or electric current to enhance radical generation [N1-R4][N2-F2].
- **Sulfate-radical-based AOPs**: These are a separate class of AOPs, where SO4•− is the dominant radical, and the evidence compares them with HR-AOPs [N2-F2].
- **Electrochemical AOPs**: These include anodic oxidation, electro-Fenton, peroxycoagulation, anodic Fenton, and electro-peroxone, and they are included in the evidence as part of the broader AOP family [N2-F2][N6-R2].

For refractory or persistent contaminants, certain AOPs are more suitable. The evidence explicitly states that SR-AOP can be more effective than HR-AOP in some cases, especially because SR-AOP can overcome some limitations of HR-AOP such as acidic pH and radical scavenging by natural organic matter [N2-F2]. The same source also notes that SR-AOP has high oxidation potential and may perform better in wider pH ranges, which is an important advantage for refractory pollutants [N2-F2]. Additionally, the real-case study on paper mill wastewater shows that Fenton oxidation can achieve substantial COD reduction and significant organic matter mineralization, suggesting that Fenton and related AOPs are well suited to refractory organics [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The evidence also supports that AOPs are used specifically for refractory organic pollutants in paper mill wastewater [N3-R4].

In summary, the most frequently used AOP types are ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOPs, with Fenton, photo-Fenton, UV/H2O2, ozone, and electro-Fenton being especially common [N1-R3][N1-R4]. They generate •OH, singlet oxygen, superoxide, persulfate-derived radicals, and sulfate radicals, and they oxidize pollutants through radical attack [N1-F1][N2-F2]. For refractory or persistent contaminants, SR-AOP and Fenton/photo-Fenton are especially relevant because they can operate under less acidic conditions and are effective against recalcitrant organics [N2-F2][N4-F3].

Branch report on practical implementation and limitations

The practical implementation of AOPs depends on several key operating conditions, the most important of which are pH, temperature, and matrix constituents. The evidence explicitly states that the major conditions to be considered in water treatment include pH, salinity, temperature, and matrix constituents, and that these conditions have a wide span [N5-R2]. It also notes that many materials with high catalytic activity at the laboratory bench scale promise AOP operation under neutral pH conditions [N5-R1]. This implies that pH is a critical design parameter, with some AOPs being optimized for acidic or neutral environments [N5-R1][N5-R2].

Temperature also matters because AOPs are generally carried out in a low-temperature range, with one source stating that Fenton oxidation is carried out in an acidic medium (pH 2.5–4.5) and low temperature (30–50 °C) [N5-R5]. The review also emphasizes that standardized experimental procedures are not available for most AOPs, and that lab-scale evaluation should include comparable and scalable parameters such as UV fluence or ozone consumption [N5-F4]. This means that temperature, along with other operational variables, must be carefully controlled and documented for reproducibility and upscaling.

Major limitations include cost, byproduct formation, and energy use. The evidence states that many novel AOP variants have not been transitioned to pilot- and full-scale operation, partly because of inconsistent experimental approaches and high energy demand [N5-F4]. It also notes that AOP studies often lack critical information needed for sound evaluation in real water matrices, including chemical and energy demand [N5-F4]. In addition, the general AOP review says that some AOPs are being explored and developed at lab scale, while others are tested at pilot scale, indicating that full-scale implementation is still limited [N1-F1]. For paper mill wastewater, the real-case study on Fenton oxidation reports that post-treatment sludge contains iron and other metals, and that the sludge should be managed as scheduled hazardous waste under Malaysian regulations [N4-F3]. This shows that byproduct formation and waste management are important operational concerns.

Process design choices trade off efficiency versus feasibility. The evidence suggests that process design must balance effectiveness with practicality. For example, the review notes that many novel AOPs are debatable for water treatment because of toxicity, lack of long-term stability, or high energy demand [N5-F4]. It also argues that flaws in experimental design can hinder translation to pilot- and full-scale demonstration [N5-F4]. This means that while some AOPs can achieve high mineralization or contaminant degradation, they may be too expensive, too energy-intensive, or too difficult to scale up for routine industrial use [N5-F4][N5-R3].

Another limitation is that AOPs are often not designed for partial oxidation alone. The evidence says that ozonation is sometimes used as a reference process for oxidative mineralization, but a typical treatment target for ozonation is partial oxidation followed by biofiltration, with significantly lower ozone dosage and energy demand [N5-F4]. This suggests that AOPs intended for complete mineralization may require higher oxidant doses and more energy than simpler oxidation processes. In the context of paper mill wastewater, the real-case study shows that Fenton oxidation can achieve substantial COD reduction and significant organic matter mineralization, but the process also generates iron-rich sludge that requires careful management [N4-F3]. This illustrates how efficiency in contaminant removal can come at the cost of higher operational and environmental burden.

Overall, the key operating conditions are pH, temperature, and matrix composition [N5-R2][N5-R5], while the major limitations are cost, byproduct formation, and energy use [N5-F4]. Process design must therefore be optimized to maximize contaminant removal and mineralization while minimizing operational complexity, waste, and energy demand [N5-F4][N5-R3].

Branch report on specific pulp/paper AOP configurations and operating examples

The most commonly used AOP configurations in pulp and paper mills, based on the evidence, are Fenton oxidation, photo-Fenton, UV/H2O2, and ozone-based treatments. The evidence explicitly lists these as common AOP configurations: Fenton and photo-Fenton systems, ozone/UV, TiO2/UV photocatalysis, and Electro-Fenton systems [N1-R4]. It also states that AOPs such as ozone, UV/H2O2, TiO2-assisted photocatalysis, ozonation, Fenton, photo-Fenton, hydrogen peroxide, and electro-oxidation have been used [N1-R3]. For pulp and paper wastewater specifically, a case study reports Fenton oxidation as a practical primary treatment for raw paper mill wastewater [N4-F3], and another study mentions UV/H2O2 oxidation, Fenton, and electrochemical oxidation as part of advanced oxidation processes [N6-R2]. The evidence also notes that ozone and hydrogen peroxide were effective in reducing color in mill effluents, with color reduction up to 87% in caustic extract and 88% in acid waste [N4-R5].

These configurations are applied to both raw and treated mill wastewater. The real-case study on raw paper mill wastewater is a direct example of Fenton oxidation being used on raw effluent, where COD and TOC were reduced and organic matter was mineralized [N4-F3]. The same study also reports that post-treatment sludge contains iron and other metals, indicating that Fenton is not only used on raw wastewater but also generates byproducts that must be managed [N4-F3]. For treated mill wastewater, the evidence shows that advanced oxidation processes are used on biorefractory RO retentate from a paper mill [N4-R3], and that UV/H2O2 and Fenton are among the AOPs applied to treated wastewater streams [N4-R3][N6-R2]. The evidence also indicates that photo-Fenton is an attractive treatment technology for wastewater containing refractory organics [N6-R3].

Performance outcomes reported in the literature are mixed but generally favorable. The real-case study on raw paper mill wastewater achieved 86.10% COD removal under optimized conditions (H2O2: 60.80 mmol/L, Fe²+: 6.98 mmol/L, pH 3, 209 min), and TOC decreased from 111.20 mg/L to 36.40 mg/L, indicating significant organic matter mineralization [N4-F3]. Another example states that ozone and hydrogen peroxide reduced color in caustic extract by up to 87%, in acid waste by up to 88%, and in final mill effluent [N4-R5]. This suggests that ozone-based AOPs can be highly effective for color removal in pulp and paper wastewater. The review on AOPs also notes that several promising AOPs, including conventional Fenton, photo-Fenton, and other AOPs, were used to treat biorefractory RO retentate from a paper mill [N4-R3], showing that these configurations are applied to difficult wastewater fractions beyond raw effluent.

In summary, the most commonly used pulp/paper AOP configurations are Fenton, photo-Fenton, UV/H2O2, and ozone-based treatments [N1-R3][N1-R4][N6-R2]. They are applied to both raw and treated mill wastewater, with Fenton used on raw effluent and other AOPs used on biorefractory or treated streams [N4-F3][N4-R3]. Performance outcomes include substantial COD reduction, significant organic matter mineralization, and high color removal [N4-F3][N4-R5]. These examples demonstrate that AOPs are operationally relevant in pulp and paper mills, but their success depends on process optimization and wastewater composition [N4-R1][N4-F3].

## Integrated final answer on common AOP types, mechanisms, and pulp/paper wastewater application

Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) are increasingly used to treat wastewater from pulp and paper mills because these effluents contain refractory organics, high chemical oxygen demand (COD), chlorinated organics, and other persistent pollutants that conventional treatment alone cannot fully remove [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. The branch reports show that pulp and paper mill wastewater is especially challenging because it contains high cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and chlorinated organic matter, with medium- to high-molecular-weight organic material and AOX (adsorbable organic halides) as major components [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. Conventional treatment is insufficient because recalcitrant organics and chlorinated contaminants resist biodegradation, and many studies explicitly state that AOPs are used to deal with refractory organic pollutants [N3-R4][N4-F3]. AOPs are therefore needed to mineralize or oxidize these pollutants, particularly chlorinated organics and other recalcitrant materials [N3-R2][N3-R4].

### Common AOP types and their chemical functions

The most frequently used AOP types in wastewater treatment are ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOP variants [N1-R4]. Common configurations include Fenton and photo-Fenton systems, ozone/UV, TiO2/UV photocatalysis, and Electro-Fenton systems [N1-R4]. A broader family of AOPs also includes ozone, UV/H2O2, TiO2-assisted photocatalysis, ozonation, Fenton, photo-Fenton, hydrogen peroxide, and electro-oxidation [N1-R3]. These are the dominant categories in the literature, and they are also the most relevant for industrial wastewater treatment [N1-R3][N1-R4].

The chemical functions of these AOPs depend on the reactive species they generate. Most AOPs produce hydroxyl radicals (•OH), which are the major radical in most AOPs [N1-F1][N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that reactive oxygen species (ROS), including singlet oxygen, superoxide, and radicals derived from persulfate, carbonate, or nitrate, may be involved [N1-F1][N5-F4]. In addition, sulfate radicals (SO4•−) are a major pathway in AOPs, and the evidence explicitly compares hydroxyl-radical-based AOPs (HR-AOP) with sulfate-radical-based AOPs (SR-AOP) [N2-F2]. This means that AOPs are not limited to •OH; sulfate radicals are also important, especially in SR-AOP systems [N2-F2].

Each process oxidizes pollutants through radical attack. The general AOP definition emphasizes that AOPs use in situ generated highly reactive radicals for oxidative degradation of contaminants [N1-F1]. The evidence further explains that radicals can be generated through various means, including ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOPs, and that AOPs can be broadly classified into four categories: ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOPs [N1-F1][N1-R4]. In practice, the most important mechanisms are:

- **Fenton and photo-Fenton**: These generate •OH from H2O2 and Fe²+ [N1-R3][N2-F2]. Fenton oxidation is explicitly mentioned as a primary treatment technology in paper mill wastewater [N4-R1][N4-F3].
- **UV/H2O2 (UV/peroxide)**: This is a classic AOP configuration, and the evidence lists it as a common AOP alongside Fenton and photo-Fenton [N1-R3][N1-R4]. It is also used in paper mill wastewater treatment [N4-R3][N4-R5].
- **Ozone-based AOPs**: Ozone is a central AOP oxidant, and the evidence explicitly states that ozone-based processes are among the common AOP categories [N1-F1][N1-R3].
- **Photo-Fenton and electro-Fenton**: These are catalytic AOP variants that use light or electric current to enhance radical generation [N1-R4][N2-F2].
- **Sulfate-radical-based AOPs**: These are a separate class of AOPs, where SO4•− is the dominant radical, and the evidence compares them with HR-AOPs [N2-F2].
- **Electrochemical AOPs**: These include anodic oxidation, electro-Fenton, peroxycoagulation, anodic Fenton, and electro-peroxone, and they are included in the broader AOP family [N2-F2][N6-R2].

For refractory or persistent contaminants, certain AOPs are more suitable. The evidence explicitly states that SR-AOP can be more effective than HR-AOP in some cases, especially because SR-AOP can overcome some limitations of HR-AOP such as acidic pH and radical scavenging by natural organic matter [N2-F2]. It also notes that SR-AOP has high oxidation potential and may perform better in wider pH ranges, which is an important advantage for refractory pollutants [N2-F2]. In addition, the real-case study on paper mill wastewater shows that Fenton oxidation can achieve substantial COD reduction and significant organic matter mineralization, suggesting that Fenton and related AOPs are well suited to refractory organics [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The evidence also supports that AOPs are used specifically for refractory organic pollutants in paper mill wastewater [N3-R4].

### Why AOPs are needed for pulp and paper wastewater

Pulp and paper mill effluent is especially difficult to treat because it contains high-COD, high-molecular-weight organics and chlorinated organics [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. The evidence explicitly states that pulp and paper mills produce high-strength wastewater with elevated COD and recalcitrant organics that are difficult to treat by conventional methods [N4-F3]. Another source says that advanced oxidation processes are used to deal with a large number of refractory organic pollutants [N3-R4]. This implies that conventional biological or physical-chemical treatment alone cannot achieve sufficient mineralization or removal of the persistent organic load in paper mill wastewater [N3-R2][N3-R4].

AOPs are needed because they address these specific pollutants through radical-based oxidation. The evidence shows that AOPs are used for oxidative degradation of contaminants, including chlorinated organics [N1-R2][N4-F3]. In the case of pulp and paper wastewater, Fenton-based treatment was reported to substantially reduce organic-matter indicators, indicating that AOPs can break down the refractory organics that conventional treatment cannot [N4-R1]. The real-case study on raw paper mill wastewater also found significant organic matter mineralization rather than simple phase transfer after Fenton oxidation, which is a strong indicator that AOPs are effective against persistent organic pollutants [N4-F3]. For chlorinated organics, AOPs are especially relevant because they generate reactive radicals that can oxidize halogenated compounds, including AOX, which are difficult to remove with conventional methods [N3-R2][N3-R5].

### Practical implementation and limitations

The practical implementation of AOPs depends on several key operating conditions, the most important of which are pH, temperature, and matrix constituents [N5-R2]. The evidence explicitly states that many materials with high catalytic activity at the laboratory bench scale promise AOP operation under neutral pH conditions [N5-R1]. This implies that pH is a critical design parameter, with some AOPs being optimized for acidic or neutral environments [N5-R1][N5-R2].

Temperature also matters because AOPs are generally carried out in a low-temperature range, with one source stating that Fenton oxidation is carried out in an acidic medium (pH 2.5–4.5) and low temperature (30–50 °C) [N5-R5]. The review also emphasizes that standardized experimental procedures are not available for most AOPs, and that lab-scale evaluation should include comparable and scalable parameters such as UV fluence or ozone consumption [N5-F4]. This means that temperature, along with other operational variables, must be carefully controlled and documented for reproducibility and upscaling.

Major limitations include cost, byproduct formation, and energy use. The evidence states that many novel AOP variants have not been transitioned to pilot- and full-scale operation, partly because of inconsistent experimental approaches and high energy demand [N5-F4]. It also notes that AOP studies often lack critical information needed for sound evaluation in real water matrices, including chemical and energy demand [N5-F4]. In addition, the general AOP review says that some AOPs are being explored and developed at lab scale, while others are tested at pilot scale, indicating that full-scale implementation is still limited [N1-F1]. For paper mill wastewater, the real-case study on Fenton oxidation reports that post-treatment sludge contains iron and other metals, and that the sludge should be managed as scheduled hazardous waste under Malaysian regulations [N4-F3]. This shows that byproduct formation and waste management are important operational concerns.

Process design choices trade off efficiency versus feasibility. The evidence suggests that process design must balance effectiveness with practicality. For example, the review notes that many novel AOPs are debatable for water treatment because of toxicity, lack of long-term stability, or high energy demand [N5-F4]. It also argues that flaws in experimental design can hinder translation to pilot- and full-scale demonstration [N5-F4]. This means that while some AOPs can achieve high mineralization or contaminant degradation, they may be too expensive, too energy-intensive, or too difficult to scale up for routine industrial use [N5-F4][N5-R3].

### Specific pulp/paper AOP configurations and operating examples

The most commonly used pulp and paper AOP configurations, based on the evidence, are Fenton oxidation, photo-Fenton, UV/H2O2, and ozone-based treatments [N1-R3][N1-R4][N6-R2]. The evidence explicitly lists these as common AOP configurations: Fenton and photo-Fenton systems, ozone/UV, TiO2/UV photocatalysis, and Electro-Fenton systems [N1-R4]. It also states that AOPs such as ozone, UV/H2O2, TiO2-assisted photocatalysis, ozonation, Fenton, photo-Fenton, hydrogen peroxide, and electro-oxidation have been used [N1-R3]. For pulp and paper wastewater specifically, a case study reports Fenton oxidation as a practical primary treatment for raw paper mill wastewater [N4-F3], and another study mentions UV/H2O2 oxidation, Fenton, and electrochemical oxidation as part of advanced oxidation processes [N6-R2]. The evidence also notes that ozone and hydrogen peroxide were effective in reducing color in mill effluents, with color reduction up to 87% in caustic extract and 88% in acid waste [N4-R5].

These configurations are applied to both raw and treated mill wastewater. The real-case study on raw paper mill wastewater is a direct example of Fenton oxidation being used on raw effluent, where COD and TOC were reduced and organic matter was mineralized [N4-F3]. The same study also reports that post-treatment sludge contains iron and other metals, indicating that Fenton is not only used on raw wastewater but also generates byproducts that must be managed [N4-F3]. For treated mill wastewater, the evidence shows that advanced oxidation processes are used on biorefractory RO retentate from a paper mill [N4-R3], and that UV/H2O2 and Fenton are among the AOPs applied to treated wastewater streams [N4-R3][N6-R2]. The evidence also indicates that photo-Fenton is an attractive treatment technology for wastewater containing refractory organics [N6-R3].

Performance outcomes reported in the literature are mixed but generally favorable. The real-case study on raw paper mill wastewater achieved 86.10% COD removal under optimized conditions (H2O2: 60.80 mmol/L, Fe²+: 6.98 mmol/L, pH 3, 209 min), and TOC decreased from 111.20 mg/L to 36.40 mg/L, indicating significant organic matter mineralization [N4-F3]. Another example states that ozone and hydrogen peroxide reduced color in caustic extract by up to 87%, in acid waste by up to 88%, and in final mill effluent [N4-R5]. This suggests that ozone-based AOPs can be highly effective for color removal in pulp and paper wastewater. The review on AOPs also notes that several promising AOPs, including conventional Fenton, photo-Fenton, and other AOPs, were used to treat biorefractory RO retentate from a paper mill [N4-R3], showing that these configurations are applied to difficult wastewater fractions beyond raw effluent.

### Summary

In short, the common AOP types used for pulp and paper wastewater are **ozone-based**, **radiation-driven**, **catalytic**, and **other AOP variants**, with **Fenton**, **photo-Fenton**, **UV/H2O2**, and **ozone-based treatments** being especially common [N1-R3][N1-R4]. These AOPs work by generating reactive species such as **hydroxyl radicals (•OH)**, **sulfate radicals (SO4•−)**, and other ROS, which oxidize pollutants through radical attack [N1-F1][N2-F2]. For refractory or persistent contaminants, **SR-AOP** and **Fenton/photo-Fenton** are especially relevant because they can operate under less acidic conditions and are effective against recalcitrant organics [N2-F2][N4-F3].

For pulp and paper wastewater, AOPs are needed because the effluent contains high-COD, high-molecular-weight organics, chlorinated organics, and AOX, and conventional treatment is insufficient to remove them effectively [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. AOPs address these pollutants by mineralizing or oxidizing them, with Fenton oxidation shown to achieve substantial COD reduction and significant organic matter mineralization in raw paper mill wastewater [N4-R1][N4-F3]. However, AOPs also have practical limitations, including sensitivity to pH and temperature, byproduct formation, and high energy and cost demands [N5-R2][N5-R5][N5-F4]. Process design choices therefore need to balance efficiency with feasibility, because some promising AOPs remain difficult to scale up or may produce hazardous byproducts that require careful management [N5-F4][N4-F3].

Overall, AOPs are a well-established and increasingly important family of technologies for pulp and paper wastewater treatment, but their success depends on choosing the right configuration, operating conditions, and wastewater composition [N4-R1][N4-F3][N4-R5].

Branch report on pulp/paper wastewater and why AOPs are needed

Pulp and paper mill effluent contains a complex mixture of organic and inorganic contaminants, with a strong emphasis on refractory organics. The evidence indicates that pulp and paper mills liberate wastewater composed of high cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, and that effluents have elevated biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), chemical oxygen demand (COD), and chlorinated chemicals [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The EPA-related source also highlights AOX (adsorbable organic halides), a bulk parameter measuring total chlorinated organic matter in wastewater [N3-R5]. Taken together, the main contaminants are lignin-derived organics, cellulose/hemicellulose fragments, high-COD organics, and chlorinated organics, especially chlorinated organic halides [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

Conventional treatment is insufficient because these contaminants are recalcitrant, persistent, and often toxic. The evidence explicitly states that pulp and paper mills produce high-strength wastewater with elevated COD and recalcitrant organics that are difficult to treat by conventional methods [N4-F3]. Another source says that advanced oxidation processes are used to deal with a large number of refractory organics pollutants [N3-R4]. This implies that conventional biological or physical-chemical treatment alone cannot achieve sufficient mineralization or removal of the persistent organic load in paper mill wastewater [N3-R2][N3-R4]. In particular, chlorinated organics and AOX are problematic because they resist biodegradation and can accumulate or persist in treatment systems [N3-R2][N3-R5].

AOPs are needed because they address these specific pollutants through radical-based oxidation. The evidence shows that AOPs are used for oxidative degradation of contaminants, including chlorinated organics [N1-R2][N4-F3]. In the case of pulp and paper wastewater, Fenton-based treatment was reported to substantially reduce organic-matter indicators, indicating that AOPs can break down the refractory organics that conventional treatment cannot [N4-R1]. The real-case study on raw paper mill wastewater also found significant organic matter mineralization rather than simple phase transfer after Fenton oxidation, which is a strong indicator that AOPs are effective against persistent organic pollutants [N4-F3]. For chlorinated organics, AOPs are especially relevant because they generate reactive radicals that can oxidize halogenated compounds, including AOX, which are difficult to remove with conventional methods [N3-R2][N3-R5]. The branch evidence also supports the idea that AOPs are used specifically for refractory organic pollutants in paper mill wastewater [N3-R4].

Overall, pulp/paper wastewater is challenging because it contains high-COD, high-molecular-weight organics and chlorinated organics, and conventional treatment is insufficient to remove them effectively. AOPs are needed because they can mineralize recalcitrant organics and oxidize chlorinated contaminants, making them a practical choice for this type of wastewater [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4][N4-F3].
branch_outputs.N7:
Branch report on common AOP types and their chemical functions

The most frequently used AOP types in wastewater treatment are ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOP variants, with the evidence explicitly stating that common AOP configurations include Fenton and photo-Fenton systems, in addition to ozone/UV, TiO2/UV photocatalysis, and Electro-Fenton systems [N1-R4]. The general review also lists ozone, UV/H2O2, TiO2-assisted photocatalysis, ozonation, Fenton, photo-Fenton, hydrogen peroxide, and electro-oxidation as AOP examples [N1-R3]. These are therefore the most commonly used categories in wastewater treatment literature [N1-R3][N1-R4].

The chemical functions of these AOPs depend on the reactive species they generate. Most AOPs produce hydroxyl radicals (•OH), which are the major radicals in most AOPs [N1-F1][N5-F4]. The review also notes that reactive oxygen species (ROS), including singlet oxygen, superoxide, and radicals derived from persulfate, carbonate, or nitrate, may be involved [N1-F1][N5-F4]. In addition to •OH, sulfate radicals (SO4•−) are also a major pathway in AOPs, and the evidence explicitly compares hydroxyl-radical-based AOPs (HR-AOP) with sulfate-radical-based AOPs (SR-AOP) [N2-F2]. This means that AOPs are not limited to •OH; sulfate radicals are also important, especially in SR-AOP systems [N2-F2].

Each process oxidizes pollutants through radical attack. The general AOP definition emphasizes that AOPs use in situ generated highly reactive radicals for oxidative degradation of contaminants [N1-F1]. The evidence further explains that radicals can be generated through various means, including ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOPs, and that AOPs can be broadly classified into four categories: ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOPs [N1-F1][N1-R4]. In practice, the most important mechanisms are:

- **Fenton and photo-Fenton**: These generate •OH from H2O2 and Fe²+ [N1-R3][N2-F2]. Fenton oxidation is explicitly mentioned as a primary treatment technology in paper mill wastewater, with evidence showing its ability to reduce COD and organic matter [N4-R1][N4-F3].
- **UV/H2O2 (UV/peroxide)**: This is a classic AOP configuration, and the evidence lists it as a common AOP alongside Fenton and photo-Fenton [N1-R3][N1-R4]. It is also used in paper mill wastewater treatment, including in studies of biorefractory retentate and raw effluent [N4-R3][N4-R5].
- **Ozone-based AOPs**: Ozone is a central AOP oxidant, and the evidence explicitly states that ozone-based processes are among the common AOP categories [N1-F1][N1-R3].
- **Photo-Fenton and electro-Fenton**: These are catalytic AOP variants that use light or electric current to enhance radical generation [N1-R4][N2-F2].
- **Sulfate-radical-based AOPs**: These are a separate class of AOPs, where SO4•− is the dominant radical, and the evidence compares them with HR-AOPs [N2-F2].
- **Electrochemical AOPs**: These include anodic oxidation, electro-Fenton, peroxycoagulation, anodic Fenton, and electro-peroxone, and they are included in the evidence as part of the broader AOP family [N2-F2][N6-R2].

For refractory or persistent contaminants, certain AOPs are more suitable. The evidence explicitly states that SR-AOP can be more effective than HR-AOP in some cases, especially because SR-AOP can overcome some limitations of HR-AOP such as acidic pH and radical scavenging by natural organic matter [N2-F2]. The same source also notes that SR-AOP has high oxidation potential and may perform better in wider pH ranges, which is an important advantage for refractory pollutants [N2-F2]. Additionally, the real-case study on paper mill wastewater shows that Fenton oxidation can achieve substantial COD reduction and significant organic matter mineralization, suggesting that Fenton and related AOPs are well suited to refractory organics [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The evidence also supports that AOPs are used specifically for refractory organic pollutants in paper mill wastewater [N3-R4].

In summary, the most frequently used AOP types are ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOPs, with Fenton, photo-Fenton, UV/H2O2, ozone, and electro-Fenton being especially common [N1-R3][N1-R4]. They generate •OH, singlet oxygen, superoxide, persulfate-derived radicals, and sulfate radicals, and they oxidize pollutants through radical attack [N1-F1][N2-F2]. For refractory or persistent contaminants, SR-AOP and Fenton/photo-Fenton are especially relevant because they can operate under less acidic conditions and are effective against recalcitrant organics [N2-F2][N4-F3].
branch_outputs.N9:
Branch report on practical implementation and limitations

The practical implementation of AOPs depends on several key operating conditions, the most important of which are pH, temperature, and matrix constituents. The evidence explicitly states that the major conditions to be considered in water treatment include pH, salinity, temperature, and matrix constituents, and that these conditions have a wide span [N5-R2]. It also notes that many materials with high catalytic activity at the laboratory bench scale promise AOP operation under neutral pH conditions [N5-R1]. This implies that pH is a critical design parameter, with some AOPs being optimized for acidic or neutral environments [N5-R1][N5-R2].

Temperature also matters because AOPs are generally carried out in a low-temperature range, with one source stating that Fenton oxidation is carried out in an acidic medium (pH 2.5–4.5) and low temperature (30–50 °C) [N5-R5]. The review also emphasizes that standardized experimental procedures are not available for most AOPs, and that lab-scale evaluation should include comparable and scalable parameters such as UV fluence or ozone consumption [N5-F4]. This means that temperature, along with other operational variables, must be carefully controlled and documented for reproducibility and upscaling.

Major limitations include cost, byproduct formation, and energy use. The evidence states that many novel AOP variants have not been transitioned to pilot- and full-scale operation, partly because of inconsistent experimental approaches and high energy demand [N5-F4]. It also notes that AOP studies often lack critical information needed for sound evaluation in real water matrices, including chemical and energy demand [N5-F4]. In addition, the general AOP review says that some AOPs are being explored and developed at lab scale, while others are tested at pilot scale, indicating that full-scale implementation is still limited [N1-F1]. For paper mill wastewater, the real-case study on Fenton oxidation reports that post-treatment sludge contains iron and other metals, and that the sludge should be managed as scheduled hazardous waste under Malaysian regulations [N4-F3]. This shows that byproduct formation and waste management are important operational concerns.

Process design choices trade off efficiency versus feasibility. The evidence suggests that process design must balance effectiveness with practicality. For example, the review notes that many novel AOPs are debatable for water treatment because of toxicity, lack of long-term stability, or high energy demand [N5-F4]. It also argues that flaws in experimental design can hinder translation to pilot- and full-scale demonstration [N5-F4]. This means that while some AOPs can achieve high mineralization or contaminant degradation, they may be too expensive, too energy-intensive, or too difficult to scale up for routine industrial use [N5-F4][N5-R3].

Another limitation is that AOPs are often not designed for partial oxidation alone. The evidence says that ozonation is sometimes used as a reference process for oxidative mineralization, but a typical treatment target for ozonation is partial oxidation followed by biofiltration, with significantly lower ozone dosage and energy demand [N5-F4]. This suggests that AOPs intended for complete mineralization may require higher oxidant doses and more energy than simpler oxidation processes. In the context of paper mill wastewater, the real-case study shows that Fenton oxidation can achieve substantial COD reduction and significant organic matter mineralization, but the process also generates iron-rich sludge that requires careful management [N4-F3]. This illustrates how efficiency in contaminant removal can come at the cost of higher operational and environmental burden.

Overall, the key operating conditions are pH, temperature, and matrix composition [N5-R2][N5-R5], while the major limitations are cost, byproduct formation, and energy use [N5-F4]. Process design must therefore be optimized to maximize contaminant removal and mineralization while minimizing operational complexity, waste, and energy demand [N5-F4][N5-R3].

These configurations are applied to both raw and treated mill wastewater. The real-case study on raw paper mill wastewater is a direct example of Fenton oxidation being used on raw effluent, where COD and TOC were reduced and organic matter was mineralized [N4-F3]. The same study also reports that post-treatment sludge contains iron and other metals, indicating that Fenton is not only used on raw wastewater but also generates byproducts that must be managed [N4-F3]. For treated mill wastewater, the evidence shows that advanced oxidation processes are used on biorefractory RO retentate from a paper mill [N4-R3], and that UV/H2O2 and Fenton are among the AOPs applied to treated wastewater streams [N4-R3][N6-R2]. The evidence also indicates that photo-Fenton is an attractive treatment technology for wastewater containing refractory organics [N6-R3].

Performance outcomes reported in the literature are mixed but generally favorable. The real-case study on raw paper mill wastewater achieved 86.10% COD removal under optimized conditions (H2O2: 60.80 mmol/L, Fe²+: 6.98 mmol/L, pH 3, 209 min), and TOC decreased from 111.20 mg/L to 36.40 mg/L, indicating significant organic matter mineralization [N4-F3]. The review on AOPs also notes that several promising AOPs, including conventional Fenton, photo-Fenton, and other AOPs, were used to treat biorefractory RO retentate from a paper mill [N4-R3], showing that these configurations are applied to difficult wastewater fractions beyond raw effluent.

## Integrated final answer on common AOP types, mechanisms, and pulp/paper wastewater application

Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) are increasingly used to treat wastewater from pulp and paper mills because these effluents contain refractory organics, high chemical oxygen demand (COD), chlorinated organics, and other persistent pollutants that conventional treatment alone cannot fully remove [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. The branch reports show that pulp and paper mill wastewater is especially challenging because it contains high cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and chlorinated organic matter, with medium- to high-molecular-weight organic material and AOX (adsorbable organic halides) as major components [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. Conventional treatment is insufficient because recalcitrant organics and chlorinated contaminants resist biodegradation, and many studies explicitly state that AOPs are used to deal with refractory organic pollutants [N3-R4][N4-F3]. AOPs are therefore needed to mineralize or oxidize these pollutants, particularly chlorinated organics and other recalcitrant materials [N3-R2][N3-R4].

### Common AOP types and their chemical functions

The most frequently used AOP types in wastewater treatment are ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOP variants [N1-R4]. Common configurations include Fenton and photo-Fenton systems, ozone/UV, TiO2/UV photocatalysis, and Electro-Fenton systems [N1-R4]. A broader family of AOPs also includes ozone, UV/H2O2, TiO2-assisted photocatalysis, ozonation, Fenton, photo-Fenton, hydrogen peroxide, and electro-oxidation [N1-R3]. These are the dominant categories in the literature, and they are also the most relevant for industrial wastewater treatment [N1-R3][N1-R4].

The chemical functions of these AOPs depend on the reactive species they generate. Most AOPs produce hydroxyl radicals (•OH), which are the major radical in most AOPs [N1-F1][N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that reactive oxygen species (ROS), including singlet oxygen, superoxide, and radicals derived from persulfate, carbonate, or nitrate, may be involved [N1-F1][N5-F4]. In addition, sulfate radicals (SO4•−) are a major pathway in AOPs, and the evidence explicitly compares hydroxyl-radical-based AOPs (HR-AOP) with sulfate-radical-based AOPs (SR-AOP) [N2-F2]. This means that AOPs are not limited to •OH; sulfate radicals are also important, especially in SR-AOP systems [N2-F2].

Each process oxidizes pollutants through radical attack. The general AOP definition emphasizes that AOPs use in situ generated highly reactive radicals for oxidative degradation of contaminants [N1-F1]. The evidence further explains that radicals can be generated through various means, including ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOPs, and that AOPs can be broadly classified into four categories: ozone-based, radiation-driven, catalytic, and other AOPs [N1-F1][N1-R4]. In practice, the most important mechanisms are:

- **Fenton and photo-Fenton**: These generate •OH from H2O2 and Fe²+ [N1-R3][N2-F2]. Fenton oxidation is explicitly mentioned as a primary treatment technology in paper mill wastewater [N4-R1][N4-F3].
- **UV/H2O2 (UV/peroxide)**: This is a classic AOP configuration, and the evidence lists it as a common AOP alongside Fenton and photo-Fenton [N1-R3][N1-R4]. It is also used in paper mill wastewater treatment [N4-R3][N4-R5].
- **Ozone-based AOPs**: Ozone is a central AOP oxidant, and the evidence explicitly states that ozone-based processes are among the common AOP categories [N1-F1][N1-R3].
- **Photo-Fenton and electro-Fenton**: These are catalytic AOP variants that use light or electric current to enhance radical generation [N1-R4][N2-F2].
- **Sulfate-radical-based AOPs**: These are a separate class of AOPs, where SO4•− is the dominant radical, and the evidence compares them with HR-AOPs [N2-F2].
- **Electrochemical AOPs**: These include anodic oxidation, electro-Fenton, peroxycoagulation, anodic Fenton, and electro-peroxone, and they are included in the broader AOP family [N2-F2][N6-R2].

For refractory or persistent contaminants, certain AOPs are more suitable. The evidence explicitly states that SR-AOP can be more effective than HR-AOP in some cases, especially because SR-AOP can overcome some limitations of HR-AOP such as acidic pH and radical scavenging by natural organic matter [N2-F2]. It also notes that SR-AOP has high oxidation potential and may perform better in wider pH ranges, which is an important advantage for refractory pollutants [N2-F2]. In addition, the real-case study on paper mill wastewater shows that Fenton oxidation can achieve substantial COD reduction and significant organic matter mineralization, suggesting that Fenton and related AOPs are well suited to refractory organics [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The evidence also supports that AOPs are used specifically for refractory organic pollutants in paper mill wastewater [N3-R4].

### Why AOPs are needed for pulp and paper wastewater

Pulp and paper mill effluent is especially difficult to treat because it contains high-COD, high-molecular-weight organics and chlorinated organics [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. The evidence explicitly states that pulp and paper mills produce high-strength wastewater with elevated COD and recalcitrant organics that are difficult to treat by conventional methods [N4-F3]. Another source says that advanced oxidation processes are used to deal with a large number of refractory organic pollutants [N3-R4]. This implies that conventional biological or physical-chemical treatment alone cannot achieve sufficient mineralization or removal of the persistent organic load in paper mill wastewater [N3-R2][N3-R4].

AOPs are needed because they address these specific pollutants through radical-based oxidation. The evidence shows that AOPs are used for oxidative degradation of contaminants, including chlorinated organics [N1-R2][N4-F3]. In the case of pulp and paper wastewater, Fenton-based treatment was reported to substantially reduce organic-matter indicators, indicating that AOPs can break down the refractory organics that conventional treatment cannot [N4-R1]. The real-case study on raw paper mill wastewater also found significant organic matter mineralization rather than simple phase transfer after Fenton oxidation, which is a strong indicator that AOPs are effective against persistent organic pollutants [N4-F3]. For chlorinated organics, AOPs are especially relevant because they generate reactive radicals that can oxidize halogenated compounds, including AOX, which are difficult to remove with conventional methods [N3-R2][N3-R5].

### Practical implementation and limitations

The practical implementation of AOPs depends on several key operating conditions, the most important of which are pH, temperature, and matrix constituents [N5-R2]. The evidence explicitly states that many materials with high catalytic activity at the laboratory bench scale promise AOP operation under neutral pH conditions [N5-R1]. This implies that pH is a critical design parameter, with some AOPs being optimized for acidic or neutral environments [N5-R1][N5-R2].

Temperature also matters because AOPs are generally carried out in a low-temperature range, with one source stating that Fenton oxidation is carried out in an acidic medium (pH 2.5–4.5) and low temperature (30–50 °C) [N5-R5]. The review also emphasizes that standardized experimental procedures are not available for most AOPs, and that lab-scale evaluation should include comparable and scalable parameters such as UV fluence or ozone consumption [N5-F4]. This means that temperature, along with other operational variables, must be carefully controlled and documented for reproducibility and upscaling.

Major limitations include cost, byproduct formation, and energy use. The evidence states that many novel AOP variants have not been transitioned to pilot- and full-scale operation, partly because of inconsistent experimental approaches and high energy demand [N5-F4]. It also notes that AOP studies often lack critical information needed for sound evaluation in real water matrices, including chemical and energy demand [N5-F4]. In addition, the general AOP review says that some AOPs are being explored and developed at lab scale, while others are tested at pilot scale, indicating that full-scale implementation is still limited [N1-F1]. For paper mill wastewater, the real-case study on Fenton oxidation reports that post-treatment sludge contains iron and other metals, and that the sludge should be managed as scheduled hazardous waste under Malaysian regulations [N4-F3]. This shows that byproduct formation and waste management are important operational concerns.

Process design choices trade off efficiency versus feasibility. The evidence suggests that process design must balance effectiveness with practicality. For example, the review notes that many novel AOPs are debatable for water treatment because of toxicity, lack of long-term stability, or high energy demand [N5-F4]. It also argues that flaws in experimental design can hinder translation to pilot- and full-scale demonstration [N5-F4]. This means that while some AOPs can achieve high mineralization or contaminant degradation, they may be too expensive, too energy-intensive, or too difficult to scale up for routine industrial use [N5-F4][N5-R3].

### Specific pulp/paper AOP configurations and operating examples

The most commonly used pulp and paper AOP configurations, based on the evidence, are Fenton oxidation, photo-Fenton, UV/H2O2, and ozone-based treatments [N1-R3][N1-R4][N6-R2]. The evidence explicitly lists these as common AOP configurations: Fenton and photo-Fenton systems, ozone/UV, TiO2/UV photocatalysis, and Electro-Fenton systems [N1-R4]. It also states that AOPs such as ozone, UV/H2O2, TiO2-assisted photocatalysis, ozonation, Fenton, photo-Fenton, hydrogen peroxide, and electro-oxidation have been used [N1-R3]. For pulp and paper wastewater specifically, a case study reports Fenton oxidation as a practical primary treatment for raw paper mill wastewater [N4-F3], and another study mentions UV/H2O2 oxidation, Fenton, and electrochemical oxidation as part of advanced oxidation processes [N6-R2]. The evidence also notes that ozone and hydrogen peroxide were effective in reducing color in mill effluents, with color reduction up to 87% in caustic extract and 88% in acid waste [N4-R5].

These configurations are applied to both raw and treated mill wastewater. The real-case study on raw paper mill wastewater is a direct example of Fenton oxidation being used on raw effluent, where COD and TOC were reduced and organic matter was mineralized [N4-F3]. The same study also reports that post-treatment sludge contains iron and other metals, indicating that Fenton is not only used on raw wastewater but also generates byproducts that must be managed [N4-F3]. For treated mill wastewater, the evidence shows that advanced oxidation processes are used on biorefractory RO retentate from a paper mill [N4-R3], and that UV/H2O2 and Fenton are among the AOPs applied to treated wastewater streams [N4-R3][N6-R2]. The evidence also indicates that photo-Fenton is an attractive treatment technology for wastewater containing refractory organics [N6-R3].

Performance outcomes reported in the literature are mixed but generally favorable. The real-case study on raw paper mill wastewater achieved 86.10% COD removal under optimized conditions (H2O2: 60.80 mmol/L, Fe²+: 6.98 mmol/L, pH 3, 209 min), and TOC decreased from 111.20 mg/L to 36.40 mg/L, indicating significant organic matter mineralization [N4-F3]. Another example states that ozone and hydrogen peroxide reduced color in caustic extract by up to 87%, in acid waste by up to 88%, and in final mill effluent [N4-R5]. This suggests that ozone-based AOPs can be highly effective for color removal in pulp and paper wastewater. The review on AOPs also notes that several promising AOPs, including conventional Fenton, photo-Fenton, and other AOPs, were used to treat biorefractory RO retentate from a paper mill [N4-R3], showing that these configurations are applied to difficult wastewater fractions beyond raw effluent.

### Summary

In short, the common AOP types used for pulp and paper wastewater are **ozone-based**, **radiation-driven**, **catalytic**, and **other AOP variants**, with **Fenton**, **photo-Fenton**, **UV/H2O2**, and **ozone-based treatments** being especially common [N1-R3][N1-R4]. These AOPs work by generating reactive species such as **hydroxyl radicals (•OH)**, **sulfate radicals (SO4•−)**, and other ROS, which oxidize pollutants through radical attack [N1-F1][N2-F2]. For refractory or persistent contaminants, **SR-AOP** and **Fenton/photo-Fenton** are especially relevant because they can operate under less acidic conditions and are effective against recalcitrant organics [N2-F2][N4-F3].

For pulp and paper wastewater, AOPs are needed because the effluent contains high-COD, high-molecular-weight organics, chlorinated organics, and AOX, and conventional treatment is insufficient to remove them effectively [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. AOPs address these pollutants by mineralizing or oxidizing them, with Fenton oxidation shown to achieve substantial COD reduction and significant organic matter mineralization in raw paper mill wastewater [N4-R1][N4-F3]. However, AOPs also have practical limitations, including sensitivity to pH and temperature, byproduct formation, and high energy and cost demands [N5-R2][N5-R5][N5-F4]. Process design choices therefore need to balance efficiency with feasibility, because some promising AOPs remain difficult to scale up or may produce hazardous byproducts that require careful management [N5-F4][N4-F3].

Overall, AOPs are a well-established and increasingly important family of technologies for pulp and paper wastewater treatment, but their success depends on choosing the right configuration, operating conditions, and wastewater composition [N4-R1][N4-F3][N4-R5].
